appraisal_events.evidence: Gilberte parle de Robert « comme se détournant d’elle, mais pour aller auprès d’autres femmes »; le narrateur confirme que « beaucoup encombraient sa vie » mais les compare à « une place vainement usurpée »; puis Robert, devenu « plus élancé, plus rapide, effet contraire d’un même vice » que M. de Charlus, court aux « mauvais lieux » par « la crainte d’être vu », mû par « la fébrilité qui naît du mécontentement de soi et de l’ennui ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator turns his wife's complaint into a much harsher diagnosis: the women around Saint-Loup are a useless alibi, and his new dashing swiftness is decoded as the furtive symptom of a concealed vice, fear of being seen, self-dissatisfaction and boredom. The whole portrait locally lowers him while also weighing down Charlus as the compared term of the same vice.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Ma mémoire avait perdu l’amour d’Albertine »; il ne subsiste qu’« une mémoire involontaire des membres, pâle et stérile imitation de l’autre »; le narrateur appelle « Albertine » en croyant que « mon amie défunte était couchée auprès de moi ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Albertine survives in the passage only as a reflex of the sleeper's arm reaching for a bell, explicitly stripped of thought, dream and love; the narrator frames this residual bodily memory as pale, sterile and quasi-vegetal, which locally reduces her to an inert trace rather than a loved presence.

status_effects.explanation: The passage is organized around exposing Saint-Loup: his marriage neglected, his women a useless screen, his elegance reinterpreted as furtive concealment of vice.
He is shown driven by fear of malevolent eyes, self-dissatisfaction and boredom, a feverish agitation that leaves him no leverage over anyone in the scene.
She is positioned as the wife turned away from, confiding her husband's defection during the walks; the narrator confirms rather than contests her grievance.
Charlus serves as the coarsened yardstick of the comparison, having grown heavy under the same vice, so the diminishing diagnosis reaches him too.
Her name is spoken only by mistake, out of a numb limb's habit, and the narrator states outright that his memory has lost the love of her.
Waking to call a dead woman's name from a reflex he no longer feels, he is left with a hollow, involuntary attachment rather than either living love or clean release.

ambiguities: The direction of Saint-Loup's diminishment shifts mid-passage: Gilberte reports desertion for other women, and the narrator both confirms it (« beaucoup encombraient sa vie ») and undercuts it by likening those women to a useless defence and a vainly usurped place, so the reproach moves from infidelity toward a concealed vice named only obliquely (« effet contraire d’un même vice », « mauvais lieux »).

The Albertine awakening admits a second reading in which the loss of love is a release for the narrator rather than a diminishment; the reading taken here follows the passage's own clinical, melancholy framing (« pâle et stérile imitation », « mon amie défunte »), which offers no note of renewal.
